There's a moment in every library, around four in the afternoon, when the light comes in low and horizontal and catches the dust suspended in the air. For a second, the dust isn't dust—it's a slow galaxy, made of everything that has drifted off the pages of books for decades: paper fibers, flecks of old binding glue, and if you want to be romantic about it, the shed particles of other people's attention. Everyone who ever read these books left something behind, or carried something away, and the exchange is visible only in that slanted light.

I think most of the world exists like this—fully present, entirely unnoticed. The grain of wood beneath varnish. The hum of a refrigerator, which you hear only when it stops. Other people's interior lives, running continuously beside ours like rivers under ice. We pass through rooms full of unattended galaxies all day long.

Maybe attention is the only real currency. Not money, not even time—time passes whether you watch it or not. But attention is spent, deliberately or not, on exactly one thing at a time. To notice the dust is almost to pay it into existence. The unattended world remains a rumor.

This is why it strikes me as strange when people say nothing happened on an ordinary day. Everything happened. Most of it just happened quietly, at an angle, in light that comes in low and won't last—won't last, that is, until tomorrow around four, when it comes slanting back to find us again.
